title: Adam's du'a
hook: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves (7:23)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jannah, and your line: their greeting is peace. Did three people get a real salam? The great themes are done. Now, eight days with the prophets' own prayers, starting where the garden story starts. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

A plate in pieces on the kitchen floor, and two people standing over it. Before anyone reaches for a broom, somebody speaks. Two sentences are always waiting in that moment. It wasn't my fault. Or: that was me. In the Qur'an's garden story, two creatures get something badly wrong, and each reaches for one of those two sentences. One of them argues his case. The other, Adam, with his wife beside him, turns his sentence into a prayer. That prayer is where these days of the prophets' du'as begin.
screen: `NOT MY FAULT, OR THAT WAS ME?`

segments.voice: Surah al-A'raf tells it. Iblis is commanded to bow to Adam and refuses. His reason: I am better than him; You made me from fire and him from clay. Later, sent out, he says: because You have led me astray. Blame upward, blame outward. Then Adam and his wife eat from the tree they'd been told to leave alone. And in verse twenty-three, in Pickthall's translation: "They said: Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If Thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!" Notice three things. First, they. Both of them pray it together; the Qur'an doesn't put the blame on her. Second, ourselves. Not Satan, who whispered to them, not the tree, not each other. The wrong is named as damage done to their own souls. Third, the request is only forgiveness and mercy, with nothing bargained. Al-Baqarah says Adam received words from his Lord, and Allah turned to him in forgiveness. Some commentators say those words were this very prayer: Allah taught Adam how to come back, and then accepted it. In Islamic teaching, that forgiveness closed the matter. The Qur'an says no soul carries another's burden, so Adam's children are each born free of his slip. The garden story ends, in the Qur'an, not with a curse but with a returned prayer. Du'a, the word for this kind of personal prayer, means a call. Adam's call is three words long at its heart: rabbana zalamna anfusana.

The practice: say it once. Sit quietly, and let one recent wrong of yours come to mind. Small is fine. Notice the excuse that usually comes with it, and set the excuse down beside you. Now, if you pray, say Adam's words once, slowly: rabbana zalamna anfusana, our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If you don't pray, say the plain version to yourself: that was mine. Then breathe, and let the rest of the sit be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Adam's du'a. Rabbana zalamna anfusana: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. A prayer that owns the wrong, answered with forgiveness. Today's word.
Your line: we wronged ourselves. Today, the next time something goes wrong that was partly yours, say so first, before any explanation. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims learn Adam's du'a (7:23) as one of the Qur'an's prayers for forgiveness; some say it in the prostration or after the prayer.

fork.setup: you're Adam. you and your wife have eaten from the tree. what do you say?
options: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.
Iblis tricked us; it was him.
fork.reveal: they own it together, ask only for forgiveness and mercy, and Allah turns to them (7:23; 2:37).

original.note: Arabic, 7:23: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.

trapdoor: what you thought: Adam's story is about a fall.
what it means: it ends with a prayer: we have wronged ourselves; forgive us, and Allah turns to them.
what a scholar hears: some commentators read the words of 2:37 as 7:23 itself; Iblis blames, Adam owns, and Islamic teaching holds no inherited sin.

notes: Pickthall wording of 7:23 quoted from memory; please confirm.
'Three words long at its heart' counts rabbana / zalamna / anfusana; confirm.
Iblis's 'because You have led me astray' paraphrases 7:16; confirm.
The statement on no inherited sin is given as Islamic teaching only, with no comparison to other traditions.
